theory.overview: Registers are the fastest and most frequently accessed memory in a computer, located directly within the processor. They serve as temporary holding places for data being processed, addresses being accessed, and control information guiding execution. Unlike main memory (RAM) which can take hundreds of clock cycles to access, registers respond instantly. Counters—specialized registers that increment or decrement—drive sequencing, timing, and program flow. Understanding how these fundamental components work is essential for grasping how processors execute instructions and manage state.

sections.title: The Role of Registers
sections.content: Registers are the working memory of the CPU. Modern processors typically have dozens to hundreds of general-purpose registers for holding data, plus special-purpose registers for specific functions: the Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction, the Instruction Register (IR) holds the currently executing instruction, the Stack Pointer (SP) tracks the top of the call stack, and status registers hold condition flags. Accessing a register takes zero wait states—it's instantaneous relative to the clock.

types.generalPurpose: Hold operands and results (R0-R31 in ARM, eax-edx in x86)
types.statusRegister: Contains flags: Z, N, C, V, etc.

sections.title: Register Files: Organized Storage
sections.content: Processors organize registers into register files—arrays of registers with multiple read/write ports. A typical register file allows reading two registers and writing one register simultaneously every clock cycle. This multi-ported design enables the register file to supply operands to the ALU while receiving results, all in one cycle. Register files are implemented using SRAM cells with specialized read/write circuitry.

sections.title: Shift Registers: Moving Data
sections.content: A shift register moves its contents left or right on each clock pulse. Serial-in-parallel-out (SIPO) shift registers convert a stream of serial bits to parallel form. Parallel-in-serial-out (PISO) does the reverse. Shift registers are used for communication protocols, multiplication/division by 2 (shift operations), and creating delays. A circular shift register (rotate) wraps bits around, preserving all information while changing positions.

operations.logicalShiftRight: Unsigned divide by 2, fill MSB with 0
operations.arithmeticShiftRight: Signed divide by 2, preserve sign bit

sections.title: Counters: Sequencing Events
sections.content: Counters are registers that automatically increment (or decrement) on each clock cycle. Synchronous counters update all bits simultaneously using carry-lookahead logic, making them fast but complex. Asynchronous (ripple) counters chain toggle flip-flops, where each stage toggles when the previous stage falls. They're simpler but slower due to ripple delay. Counters drive the program counter (sequential instruction fetch), timers, and frequency dividers.

sections.title: The Program Counter: Guiding Execution
sections.content: The Program Counter (PC) is arguably the most important register in a processor. It holds the memory address of the next instruction to fetch. After each fetch, the PC increments by the instruction size (typically 4 bytes). For branches and jumps, the PC is loaded with a new target address. The PC's behavior—sequential with occasional jumps—defines the flow of program execution. Some architectures expose the PC as a general register (ARM), others hide it (x86).
operations: Call: PC = target, save return address

sections.title: Register Windows and Renaming
sections.content: Advanced architectures use register windows (SPARC) or register renaming to avoid limitations. Register windows provide multiple overlapping register sets for fast procedure calls. Register renaming maps architectural registers to a larger physical register file, eliminating false dependencies (WAR and WAW hazards) in out-of-order execution. These techniques allow more instruction-level parallelism while maintaining the simple programmer-visible register model.

keyConcepts.name: Register File
keyConcepts.description: Multi-ported SRAM array storing all processor registers. Supports simultaneous read/write.

keyConcepts.name: Program Counter (PC)
keyConcepts.description: Holds address of next instruction. Automatically increments, loads new value on branches.

keyConcepts.name: Shift Operation
keyConcepts.description: Moves bits left or right. Shifting left multiplies by 2; right divides by 2.

keyConcepts.name: Synchronous vs Asynchronous
keyConcepts.description: Synchronous counters update all bits together (fast). Asynchronous ripple through stages (slow).
keyConcepts.delay: Sync: O(1), Async: O(log n) or O(n)

complexity.counterDelay: O(1) for sync, O(n) for async

practiceProblems.title: Register Access Time
practiceProblems.description: How many clock cycles does a typical register read take?
practiceProblems.explanation: Register access is the fastest memory operation, completing in a single clock cycle with zero wait states.

practiceProblems.title: Shift Left Operation
practiceProblems.description: What is the result of shifting binary 00001100 left by 1 position?
practiceProblems.explanation: 12 (00001100) shifted left becomes 24 (00011000). Each left shift multiplies by 2.

practiceProblems.title: Program Counter Increment
practiceProblems.description: After fetching a 4-byte instruction, how much does the PC increment?
practiceProblems.explanation: The PC advances by the instruction size (4 bytes for ARM/x86-32) to point to the next sequential instruction.

practiceProblems.title: Counter Types
practiceProblems.description: Which counter type is faster but requires more gates?
practiceProblems.explanation: Synchronous counters use lookahead logic to update all bits simultaneously (faster). Asynchronous counters are simpler but have ripple delay.

practiceProblems.title: Modulo-16 Counter
practiceProblems.description: How many flip-flops are needed for a modulo-16 counter?
practiceProblems.explanation: A modulo-16 counter counts 0-15 (16 states). 2^4 = 16, so 4 flip-flops are needed.

practiceProblems.title: Barrel Shifter
practiceProblems.description: What is the time complexity of a shift using a barrel shifter?
practiceProblems.explanation: A barrel shifter can shift any number of positions in constant time using a matrix of multiplexers, unlike sequential shifters.
hints: Constant time regardless of shift amount

snippets.title: Register File Simulation
snippets.code:
class RegisterFile:
    def __init__(self, num_registers=32, width=32):
        self.registers = [[0] * width for _ in range(num_registers)]
        self.num_regs = num_registers
    
    def read(self, addr1, addr2=None):
        # Read two registers simultaneously
        val1 = self.registers[addr1]
        val2 = self.registers[addr2] if addr2 else None
        return val1, val2
    
    def write(self, addr, value):
        # Write one register
        if addr != 0:  # R0 often hardwired to 0
            self.registers[addr] = value
    
    def display(self):
        for i in range(min(8, self.num_regs)):
            val = sum(bit << j for j, bit in enumerate(self.registers[i]))
            print(f'R{i}: {val}')

# Shift operations
def shift_left(value, positions, width=8):
    mask = (1 << width) - 1
    return (value << positions) & mask

def shift_right_logical(value, positions):
    return value >> positions

def shift_right_arithmetic(value, positions, width=8):
    sign_bit = (value >> (width - 1)) & 1
    result = value >> positions
    if sign_bit:
        # Fill with 1s from left
        ones = ((1 << positions) - 1) << (width - positions)
        result |= ones
    return result & ((1 << width) - 1)

# Test
rf = RegisterFile(8, 8)
rf.write(1, [0,1,0,1,0,0,0,0])  # 10
rf.write(2, [1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0])  # 15
rf.display()

print(f'10 << 1 = {shift_left(10, 1)}')  # 20
print(f'10 >> 1 = {shift_right_logical(10, 1)}')  # 5
